newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan panel chief queries need to scrap stock tax.
newsitem.headline: Japan panel chief queries need to scrap stock tax.

text.p: The proposed abolition of Japan's securities transaction tax, which has been criticised as sapping market vitality, may do little to boost securities dealings, the head of the government's tax panel told Reuters on Monday.

"The call to scrap taxes, because they make securities trading inconvenient and dampen activity, sounds heroic, but the volume in securities trading is rising even now when there is a securities transaction tax. It is not a big problem," Hiroshi Kato said in an interview.
He added, however, that this was his personal opinion and did not necessarily reflect the views of the panel.

Critics say the tax not only makes share trading in Tokyo unattractive, but could encourage more firms to go abroad to do business, thus undermining efforts to revitalise the Tokyo market through deregulation.

The panel is discussing revisions to Japan's taxes, including those on securities transactions and capital gains on stocks, as part of the government's "Big Bang" financial reforms. The panel aims to reach a decision on securities and capital gains tax reforms in time to implement them in fiscal year 1998/99.
In April 1996, Japan temporarily cut the tax on securities transactions to 0.21 percent from 0.3 percent, although the reduction will lapse in March 1998 unless steps are taken to extend it.

Japan also imposes a uniform tax rate of 26 percent on capital gains on stocks, although investors can opt instead to pay a withholding tax, levied at a fixed rate of 1.05 percent on total revenues from stock sales, regardless of the amount of capital gains.
"What we should do is lower the securities transaction tax a bit for a limited time and ask the market to decide," said Kato, who is also president of Chiba University of Commerce.
"If lowering the tax increases the traded volume, then that's fine. But if we find out there is no change, there is no need to lower the tax," he said.
He added that the government is in the process of gathering data on how much the lowering of Japan's securities transaction taxes over the past two years has helped boost global securities trading.

Finance Ministry officials have said that the review of these taxes will be completed by the end of the 1997/98 fiscal year and that any changes will be implemented in the following fiscal year, which starts on April 1, 1998.

Kato said that, although taxes are often blamed for stifling Tokyo's globalisation efforts, government surveys show that foreign firms have left Japan not because of taxes, but because of high office rents and labour costs.
Japan must also decide whether to follow the European model, which emphasises taxation at the point of purchase or sale, or the American model, in which taxes are less direct, he said.
In addition, because securities can be considered as assets, they must be taxed in some way or another to maintain the fairness of the overall tax system, he said.
"It is natural to tax income. If we don't, it will be unfair. We can't just scrap this (tax)," he said.
He added that, even if a political decision leads to the abolition of the securities transaction tax, Japan must at least retain taxes on capital gains to maintain fairness within the system.
